title: Jump Game VI
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning the last k dp values every step versus combining DP with a monotonic decreasing deque.

blocks.text: You start at index 0 of a 0-indexed integer array nums, with an integer k. From index i, you may jump to any index in [i+1, min(n-1, i+k)]. Your score is the SUM of nums[j] for every index j you visit (including the start and end). Return the MAXIMUM score achievable reaching the last index.

blocks.caption: Dynamic programming (best score reaching each index) combined with a monotonic deque (for the max of the last k dp values) solves this in O(n)

blocks.text: The best score reaching index i is nums[i] PLUS the best score reaching any of the k positions immediately before it (since a jump of UP TO k steps can land on i from any of those); finding that best "immediately before" score is exactly a sliding window maximum query over the dp array itself.

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding the Best Total Score on a Path With a Maximum Jump Distance
blocks.text: Imagine hopping across stepping stones, each worth some number of points (possibly negative), where each hop can cover UP TO k stones at once. The best possible total score upon reaching any given stone is that stone's own value, PLUS whatever the best possible score was among all the stones within jumping range BEHIND it, since you could have arrived there from any one of them.

blocks.caption: dp[i] needs the maximum dp value among the last k positions; a monotonic decreasing deque tracks this maximum incrementally as the window slides forward

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: 7 (dp[5], the last index), matching the expected result

Before rescanning up to k previous dp values for EVERY position (an O(n*k) approach), notice that this "max of the last k values" query is EXACTLY the sliding window maximum problem, solvable with a monotonic decreasing deque in O(n) total.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: dp[i] (the best score reaching index i) equals nums[i] PLUS the maximum dp value among the k positions immediately before i, since a single jump of up to k steps can arrive at i from any of them.

Observation 2: As i increases by 1, the "window" of relevant previous dp values (the last k positions) also slides forward by 1, making this structurally IDENTICAL to a sliding window maximum problem, just applied to the dp array being built incrementally rather than a fixed input array.

Observation 3: A monotonic decreasing deque of indices (by dp VALUE) directly answers "what is the max dp value in the current window" in O(1), by simply reading its front.

Observation 4: As each new dp[i] is computed, it must ALSO be inserted into the deque (maintaining the decreasing order, popping any smaller values it now dominates from the back), making it available for FUTURE positions' window-maximum queries.

This is dynamic programming (dp[i] = best score reaching i) combined with a monotonic decreasing deque, which efficiently answers the "max dp value in the last k positions" query needed at every step.
Compute dp[i] directly by scanning back up to k previous positions and taking the maximum dp value among them, repeated for every index.

items: Initialize dp[0] = nums[0].
For each subsequent index i, scan the up-to-k previous positions [max(0, i-k), i-1], taking the maximum dp value among them, and set dp[i] = that maximum plus nums[i].

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Directly scanning the last k dp values for each position implements the recurrence exactly as defined, without any additional structure.
This correctly handles the "min(0, i-k)" boundary, since the window shrinks near the start of the array.

blocks.text: Correctly computes the maximum score, since it directly applies the recurrence at every step, considering all valid previous positions.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n*k), since each of the n positions rescans up to k previous dp values.
Space: O(n), for the dp array.
Limitation: O(n*k) does not scale when both n and k can be up to 10^5; a monotonic deque reduces the "max of the last k values" query to O(1) amortized, achieving O(n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rescans up to k dp values for every position. Instead, maintain a monotonic decreasing deque of indices (ordered by their dp VALUES), exactly as in Sliding Window Maximum. Before computing dp[i], evict any deque entries that have fallen outside the k-window (index < i - k). The deque's front then directly gives the maximum dp value needed. After computing dp[i], insert it into the deque, popping any now-dominated (smaller-or-equal) entries from the back first.

Initialize dp[0] = nums[0] and a deque containing index 0. For i from 1 to n-1: evict deque entries with index < i - k from the front; set dp[i] = dp[deque.front] + nums[i]; then pop entries from the deque's back while their dp value is <= dp[i], and push i. Return dp[n-1].
Combine dynamic programming with a monotonic decreasing deque, efficiently tracking the maximum dp value within the last k positions.

codes.python:
from collections import deque

def max_result(nums, k):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * n
    dp[0] = nums[0]
    window = deque([0])                                                    # monotonic DECREASING deque of indices, by dp value

    for i in range(1, n):
        while window and window[0] < i - k:                                # evict indices that have fallen OUT of the k-window
            window.popleft()
        dp[i] = dp[window[0]] + nums[i]                                    # the deque's front holds the best reachable score so far
        while window and dp[window[-1]] <= dp[i]:                          # maintain decreasing order: pop anything dp[i] now dominates
            window.pop()
        window.append(i)

    return dp[n - 1]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(max_result([1, -1, -2, 4, -7, 3], 2))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n): each index is pushed onto the deque exactly once and popped at most once (from either end) across the entire algorithm.
Space: O(k), for the deque (which never holds more than k+1 entries at once).

The deque, at any point, holds exactly the indices within the current k-window whose dp values could STILL possibly be the maximum for some future position (any index whose dp value is ALREADY dominated by a later index's dp value is immediately popped, since it can never again be the maximum going forward). This is exactly the same reasoning as the standard sliding window maximum technique, here applied to the dp array as it is being built, one value at a time, rather than to a fixed input array.

items: The deque stores INDICES (not dp values directly), so checking "is this index still within the k-window" during eviction is a simple index comparison.
Eviction happens BEFORE computing dp[i] (ensuring the window is correctly up to date), while insertion happens AFTER (since dp[i] must be fully computed before it can be added to the deque).
The final answer is simply dp[n-1], the best score reaching the very last index.

blocks.text: When a dynamic programming recurrence needs the MAXIMUM (or minimum) among the last k computed values, a monotonic deque, applied to the dp array as it is being built, reduces what would otherwise be an O(n*k) rescanning cost to O(n) total, exactly as in the classic Sliding Window Maximum technique.

items: Evicting stale deque entries AFTER computing dp[i] instead of BEFORE, which could incorrectly include an out-of-window index in the maximum calculation.
Forgetting that the deque must be updated with the NEWLY computed dp[i] value (not the raw nums[i] value), since future positions need the best CUMULATIVE score, not just the individual array value.
Using a strict comparison instead of <= when popping dominated entries from the back, potentially leaving redundant entries in the deque unnecessarily.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "DP recurrence needing the max/min of the last k computed values" points directly to combining dynamic programming with a monotonic deque.

items: How would you also RECONSTRUCT the actual path (which indices were visited), not just the maximum score? Track, alongside each dp[i], WHICH previous index it came from (the deque's front at that time), then walk backward from n-1 using those recorded predecessors.

How does this problem relate to Sliding Window Maximum directly? It is structurally the SAME sliding-window-maximum technique, just applied to a dynamically GROWING array (the dp array), rather than a fixed, pre-given input array.

What would change if jumps could go BACKWARD as well as forward? The problem would become significantly more complex, since dp[i] could then depend on LATER positions too, likely requiring a completely different approach (such as a full graph shortest-path algorithm) instead of a simple left-to-right DP.
A direct application of the monotonic deque technique from Sliding Window Maximum, here combined with dynamic programming, applied to the dp array as it is incrementally constructed.

blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n*k) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (DP + monotonic deque): O(n) time, O(k) space.
